questions.question: What must be specified before something can be called an algebraic structure?
options: One or more operations, with no set specified
A set together with an order relation on it
A set and operations already proven associative
A set and one or more operations on that set

questions.question: For the candidate structure $(\{0,1\},\oplus)$, what must $\oplus$ do to be an operation on the set?
options: It must satisfy $a\oplus b=b\oplus a$ for every pair from $\{0,1\}$
It must assign an element of $\{0,1\}$ to each pair with $a\ne b$
It must have an identity element and an inverse for each element
It must assign an element of $\{0,1\}$ to each ordered pair from $\{0,1\}$

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb{R},+)$ not the same algebraic structure as $(\mathbb{R},\cdot)$?
options: They use the same set but different operations
They use different sets but the same operation
Multiplication on $\mathbb{R}$ is not associative, unlike addition
Only $(\mathbb{R},+)$ has an identity element in $\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: Suppose $A=\{0,1\}$ and $a*b=a$ for all $a,b\in A$. Which statement correctly describes the candidate $(A,*)$?
options: It is not a structure because $A$ has only two elements
It is a field because every algebraic structure with two elements is a field
It is not a structure because the operation is not ordinary addition
It is an algebraic structure because the rule is an operation on $A$

questions.question: In the chain semigroup, monoid, group, Abelian group, each step adds one requirement. Which statement holds for every group $(A,\star)$?
options: It is also a monoid and a semigroup.
It is also an Abelian group.
It is a semigroup but need not be a monoid.
It is a monoid but no longer a semigroup.

questions.question: Before verifying any axioms, the notation $(A,+,\cdot)$ alone makes no guarantees. How should it be read?
options: As a ring, since any set with two operations is a ring.
A set $A$ with two operations whose properties need checking.
As $A$ with the usual addition and multiplication of numbers.
As a set $A$ whose two operations must be commutative.

questions.question: Let $A=\{0,1\}$ and define $a*b=a-b$ using ordinary integer subtraction. Why is $(A,*)$ not an algebraic structure with this operation on $A$?
options: Because $0*1=-1$, which is not in $A$.
Because $0*1\ne1*0$, so the rule is not commutative.
Because no $e\in A$ satisfies $e*a=a*e=a$ for all $a\in A$.
Because $0*0=1*1$, so different pairs give the same output.
